subject: Mathematics
title: Permutation and Combination
learningOutcomes: Explain and use the fundamental counting principle (rule of product) to count outcomes without listing them.
Define the factorial \(n!\), state that \(0!=1\), and simplify factorial expressions and equations.
Explain permutations and evaluate \({}^{n}P_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\); handle alike objects, circular arrangements and key-chain (necklace) arrangements.
Explain combinations and evaluate \({}^{n}C_{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\); use \({}^{n}C_{r}={}^{n}C_{n-r}\) to shorten work.
Decide correctly between permutation and combination by asking whether order matters.
Apply permutation and combination to real-world problems: number plates, seating, committees, cryptography, lottery odds and sets of songs.

sections.heading: Rule of Product (Fundamental Counting Principle)
sections.body: If one job can be done in \(m\) ways and, after it, a second job can be done in \(n\) ways, then both jobs together can be done in \(m\times n\) ways. It extends to any number of jobs: multiply the number of choices at each stage. Example: \(4\) shirts and \(3\) trousers give \(4\times3=12\) outfits.

sections.heading: Factorial Notation
sections.body: For a positive integer \(n\), \(n!=n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots3\cdot2\cdot1\), and by definition \(0!=1\). A factorial can always be opened one step: \(n!=n\,(n-1)!\). Ratios are solved by opening the larger factorial: \(\frac{8!}{5!}=\frac{8\times7\times6\times5!}{5!}=336\).

sections.heading: Permutation: order matters
sections.body: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order. The number of permutations of \(n\) different objects taken \(r\) at a time is \({}^{n}P_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\), where \(0\le r\le n\). Taking all objects, \({}^{n}P_{n}=n!\). Example: \({}^{7}P_{3}=7\times6\times5=210\).

sections.heading: Permutation when some objects are alike
sections.body: The number of different arrangements of \(n\) objects in which \(p\) are alike of one kind, \(q\) alike of another kind, and so on, is \(\frac{n!}{p!\,q!\cdots}\). Example: the letters of EVENING (7 letters, E twice, N twice) can be arranged in \(\frac{7!}{2!\,2!}=1260\) ways.

sections.heading: Circular permutation and key-chain arrangements
sections.body: Around a circle there is no fixed starting place, so \(n\) different objects can be arranged in \((n-1)!\) ways. If the circle can be turned over (a necklace or key chain), clockwise and anti-clockwise arrangements look the same and the number is \(\frac{(n-1)!}{2}\). Two persons together: treat them as one block, then multiply by \(2!\).

sections.heading: Permutation in Cryptography
sections.body: A permutation of the letter positions can be used as a secret code: the word is split into letters, the letters are labelled and then re-written in the order given by the code. Knowing the code, the receiver reverses the arrangement to recover the message. This is a real use of permutation in keeping information secure.

sections.heading: Combination: order does not matter
sections.body: A combination is a selection in which the order of the chosen objects does not matter. The number of combinations of \(n\) different objects taken \(r\) at a time is \({}^{n}C_{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}=\frac{{}^{n}P_{r}}{r!}\). Useful facts: \({}^{n}C_{0}={}^{n}C_{n}=1\) and \({}^{n}C_{r}={}^{n}C_{n-r}\). Example: \({}^{10}C_{3}=\frac{10\times9\times8}{3\times2\times1}=120\).

sections.heading: Permutation or Combination? The three decisions
sections.body: Ask in this order: (1) Does the order matter? If yes use \({}^{n}P_{r}\), if only the chosen group matters use \({}^{n}C_{r}\). (2) Are all objects different, or are some alike? (3) Is the arrangement in a line or around a circle? Trigger words: arrange, seat, line up, form numbers or words point to permutation; choose, select, committee, team, hand of cards point to combination.

definitions.definition: If jobs are done one after another in \(m\) and \(n\) ways, together they can be done in \(m\times n\) ways.
An arrangement of objects in a definite order.
A selection of objects in which the order does not matter.
Number of permutations of \(n\) different objects taken \(r\) at a time: \(\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\).
Number of combinations of \(n\) different objects taken \(r\) at a time: \(\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\).
An arrangement of objects around a circle; \(n\) different objects give \((n-1)!\) arrangements.
A circular arrangement that can be turned over; the count is \(\frac{(n-1)!}{2}\).
Objects that cannot be told apart; repeats are divided out: \(\frac{n!}{p!\,q!\cdots}\).
Writing a message in a secret code, here by re-ordering its letters with a permutation.

examTips: Ask first: does the order matter? Order matters, use \({}^{n}P_{r}\); only the group matters, use \({}^{n}C_{r}\).
Write \(\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) first, then cancel. Open only the larger factorial and let the smaller one cancel.
Remember \(0!=1\). It is the most common factorial mistake.
For "always together" tie the group into one block and multiply by the arrangements inside it. For "never together" subtract the together count from the total.
In a restricted-place question, fill the restricted place first (units digit of an even number, first digit of a number with a zero).
"At least one" is easiest as total minus none. Use \({}^{n}C_{r}={}^{n}C_{n-r}\) when \(r\) is more than half of \(n\).
